scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Socks on the Dance Floor: Southern Africa's Sokkie Tradition
This is Sokkie. 19th century to present.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Title card: Sokkie · South Africa · 19th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Sokkie originated in Southern Africa from the Afrikaner trekkers.
Over time, it developed into a major social partner dance style.
Its common name 'sokkie' (Afrikaans for 'sock') stems from the tradition of young people dancing in socks or barefoot.
on_screen: Map: South Africa · Africa
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Sokkie is performed primarily as a social dance during party gatherings, social functions, and nightclub events across Southern Africa, serving as a widespread social activity among Afrikaners.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Sokkie is a social partner ballroom dance.
Dancers combine steps from various styles such as loopdans, two-step, swing, boogie, social foxtrot, and quickstep.
It can also include the 'boerewals', which is a Viennese waltz adapted for sokkie.
Watch for Boerewals, Loopdans.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Couples traveling counter-clockwise around a social dance floor.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Sokkie is accompanied by a modern commercial genre of sokkie music as well as general pop, country, trance, and hip-hop.
Sokkie tracks are often produced by taking successful English hits and translating them into Afrikaans or adapting popular melodies.
Listen for the Synthesizer, Electronic drums, Vocals.
The pulse is 4/4 or 3/4.
Commercial Afrikaans pop music characterized by electronic dance beats, popular pop melodies, and translated catchy hooks designed for partner dance halls.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Prominent commercial sokkie music artists include Kurt Darren, Nicholis Louw, and Juanita du Plessis.
Variants and synonymous forms in Southern Africa are known locally by names such as langarm, sakkie-sakkie, kotteljons, and Water-pomp.
Derived from Afrikaner trekker social dances, sokkie evolved to incorporate steps from international ballroom genres including two-step, foxtrot, quickstep, swing, and Viennese waltz (boerewals).
